questions.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]x
$$

 with respect to $x$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$, we have

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.
$$

For a symmetric matrix $A$, the gradient of the function $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax$ with respect to $x\in {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=2Ax.
$$

Therefore, since $A$ is symmetric, we get

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=2[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)={y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot y \\  & ={A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -29\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=(Ax-2b)^{T}(Ax-2b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-2b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-2b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-2b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+2 \\ 0-4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ 0-10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
